no-vote-under-twenty-one.summary: 6.3 million fewer adults vote. No state flips. Nixon wins, 520–17–1. The closest call is Minnesota, which holds for Nixon by 5.5 points. McGovern wins in 0 of 100 draws. Low confidence. The interviews point the other way from the historical record.
assumptions: Adults aged 18 to 20 (8.1% of adults 18+ in the 1970 census [I]) are removed from the electorate in every state; the backbone has no age split, so they are taken as a uniform slice of every cell, voting like the rest of it. Young voters in fact turned out less and leaned further toward the challenger.
howIGotThis: What changed: The 26th Amendment is never ratified, so citizens aged 18 to 20 cannot vote for president in 1972.

What historians found (9 findings, strong evidence): No sourced study of a world without the 26th Amendment exists. 1972 data show 18–20s turned out about 2–3 points below 21–24s (48.3% vs 50.7%) and split roughly evenly between McGovern and Nixon, so removing them would likely have changed little. The 1970 statute might still have allowed them to vote for president.
The numbers: the 1970 and 1980 census counts interpolated to 1972 and certified returns; every draw reproduces 1972 exactly before the change.
How sure: I reran it 100 times with different population and parameter draws.
Low confidence: The interviews point the other way from the historical record.
